rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 “understanding” law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the highest court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year. If a trans visitor is arrested or detained here, the custody consequence of the lagging framework is documented rather than theoretical: facilities house inmates by their family-register (registered) sex rather than gender identity — a women's prison in one prefecture held an inmate registered female who identifies as a man, and a transgender activist was held among men for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention, initially denied hormone treatment, mocked for his identity during interrogations, and allowed to shower away from other detained men only after requests, with hormones arriving only after a doctor recommended them. Pressure over an inmate's male clothing and hairstyle went unresolved for years before a bar association issued a formal warning to the prison in September 2023.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and the capital and the second city have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

Same-sex marriage remains unavailable, which matters for a trans visitor planning to travel with a partner on spousal status. One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.

Litigation flux: the court-based gender-change route is the moving part of the legal framework — a 2023 ruling struck down the sterilisation requirement and another ruled workplace bathroom restrictions illegal the same year, while full marriage equality and violence-protection guarantees remain absent; the 2023 “understanding” law was enacted only after months of debate and watering-down amid a culture-war contest.

A dated 2009 shadow report documents invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation plus discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention at the time — a baseline for comparing how far institutional protection has moved.

Custody-policy flux surrounds the placement practice: a prefecture bar association's September 2023 formal ‘warning’ to a prison followed years with no policy change on an inmate's male clothing and hairstyle, and an international human-rights organisation (June 2025) frames the pre-trial detention of a transgender activist — held among men, initially denied hormone treatment until a doctor recommended it — within its broader criticism of the country's general pre-trial detention system, a burden every detainee faces that falls harder on a transgender detainee.

Custody axis: no national statute, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary or segregation) is documented — placement by family-register sex is established by case reporting, while any identity-based placement option and any special-unit or solitary rule are undocumented; the two prison-axis sources are press and human-rights documentation of individual cases rather than official policy texts. Detention consequences arise only if a trans visitor is arrested — rare in practice given the documented low day-to-day risk — but nothing in the record suggests a detained trans person receives protective placement, and the criticism of the general pre-trial detention system concerns all detainees rather than trans people specifically.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is among the most accepting destinations in the region for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (a long-standing local tradition of visible gender variance that long predates modern categories), the government actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in the region, and the immigration authority runs a dedicated welcome initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 gender equality act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a trans woman in a resort city highlighted — this country has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime. The gap extends into custody: because no document issued here can identify a trans woman as female, placement follows legal sex in documented cases — a trans activist who became a detainee while protesting the ruling military government in June 2015 was sent to a men's prison, told “she remains a man” and harassed during intake — while the prison authority says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993, holds transgender inmates in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men at one remand prison, and accepts that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary confinement. A trans visitor detained here therefore meets an unresolved placement practice: birth-sex men's facilities in documented cases, separated LGBT wings in others, with no guaranteed identity-matched housing.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly the country's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and transit are unproblematic.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Same-sex marriage legal since January 2025 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Custody-policy flux: after reports of abuse and the documented placement of a trans woman in a men's prison in 2015, the prison authority announced a pilot using a prison in the capital as an LGBT facility — reported in 2016-17 as a possible world-first exclusively-LGBTQ prison — which activists welcomed while fearing it “could encourage exclusion” and insisting placement “should be an option, not an obligation”; counts at the time recorded roughly a few thousand LGBT-identified people among about 300,000 prisoners (a few dozen of them transgender), with a 2017 figure of more than 6,000 registered as sexual minorities.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:

rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Scams, drink-spiking in nightlife, road safety, and petty theft affect all travellers to this country.

Custody axis: the nationwide separation practice and the dedicated block at one remand prison rest on 2016-17 press reporting, and no current official placement rule or national special-unit or solitary-practice rule for trans prisoners is documented in this record's sources; the status of the capital pilot is unresolved (reported as under discussion in 2017); and whether a detained foreign visitor would be routed like the documented resident cases is not established — so a detained trans visitor's placement cannot be assumed from the separated-wing reports.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is the most progressive destination in the region for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and the main city as a regional queer hub. The protections do not reliably reach custody: documentation shows the response to transgender-prisoner vulnerability has been isolation or segregation from the general prison population rather than placement in facilities matching gender identity, and trans women have at times been held in men's prisons — but courts have intervened case-by-case, most notably an October 2019 ruling that ordered the prison service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one.

Two traveller-specific risks pull the score down. First, the main international airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travellers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition (“If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male”). Every foreign visitor transits that airport, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people “bearing the brunt.” Anti-trans rhetoric from the national leadership is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing governing coalition and the conflict's aftermath have weakened protections, though a parliamentary security committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Dating-app traps and organized ambushes are a direct caution for trans visitors using apps.

Custody litigation flux: the 2019 corrective ruling came after a civil-rights organisation petitioned — the prisoner was initially placed in a separate wing of the women's prison, and the organisation prepared a further petition to have her housed with the general population (its outcome is not reported in this record's sources), showing that custody placement for trans prisoners is reviewed case-by-case through the courts rather than set by published rules; the isolation-based default predating that ruling is documented in a 2015 law-journal article.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:

Resident-prisoner documentation: a 2015 law-journal article documents the response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability as isolating and segregating trans inmates apart from the rest of the prison population rather than placing them in facilities matching their gender identity, describing isolation-based custody as the default management practice; a civil-society foundation (October 2019) records the court order to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one, after she was initially placed in a separate wing of the women's prison, with trans women at times held in men's prisons before such correction.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Security risks from the conflict (rockets, terrorism, border areas) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Custody axis: no statute or prison-service regulation on trans-prisoner placement is documented — the isolation/segregation pattern rests on a 2015 journal article and the corrective intervention on a single October 2019 court case, with the follow-up petition's outcome unreported — and whether case-by-case judicial relief would extend to a detained foreign visitor is not established.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is one of the most socially accepting destinations in the region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity, a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised in this country.

However, there is a “near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level”: no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), a national anti-discrimination equality bill has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. Documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue — documented incidents include bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials; partner or marriage-based protections do not exist. The vacuum extends into custody: transgender women at the capital's main city jail are held by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories — where mandatory head-shaving applies on arrival to the male dorm and safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than any gender-matched placement policy — while a second city's jail answers abuse risk by relocating LGBT detainees to a separate annex; a trans visitor arrested in this country has no documented path to identity-matched custody.
rewrites.blindTangential:
A national anti-discrimination equality bill has been stalled in the national legislature for 25 years, and no national legal gender recognition law exists; the 2025 killings are being cited by activists as an urgent reminder for the bill's passage. This is national legislation flux that may colour a visit, not a direct travel restriction.

Custody-policy flux: the documented official response is administrative segregation rather than gender-matched placement — a regional jail authority official said LGBT detainees at a second city's jail are relocated in batches to the jail annex “to prevent abuse”, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings living in the annex since its establishment (March 2023); an investigative-journalism organisation's investigation (December 2022) documents that at the capital's main city jail transgender women and gay men held in the ordinary male dormitories use informal same-sex “weddings” with male inmates as a survival and protection strategy against abuse.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The absent national legal gender recognition law, the 25-year-stalled equality bill, and the commission's lack of enforcement power are resident-facing; the 2025 killings and the earlier documented student discrimination in schools affect residents primarily.

Deep cultural traditions of gender diversity and the capital's Pride and nightlife scene are resident-facing cultural facts a visitor can observe but not rely on legally.

Resident-prisoner documentation: the investigative-journalism investigation (December 2022) records transgender women at the capital's main city jail housed by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories — where mandatory head-shaving applies on arrival to the male dorm and detainees assume housekeeping and entertainer roles — with informal same-sex “weddings” with male inmates widely used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse, and safety coming from inmate hierarchies rather than policy; a local newspaper (March 2023) records the official practice of a regional jail authority transferring LGBT detainees in batches to a city jail's annex “to prevent abuse”.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
General crime (kidnapping risks in certain provinces, scams, typhoon risks) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical treatment of identity documents at borders is not documented, and the sources do not detail how bathroom and fitting-room policies at venues are enforced.

Custody axis: no national rule on trans-prisoner placement — birth-sex vs identity housing, special units, or solitary/segregation practice — is documented; the male-dorm housing is documented at the capital's main city jail and the annex segregation at a second city's jail only, so practice appears to vary by jail; the head-shaving intake requirement applies to the male dormitory generally rather than to transgender detainees specifically, and the 2022-23 reports are the only custody sources in this record.
blindSourceSummaries: No national legal gender recognition law exists (identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender); a national anti-discrimination equality bill has been stalled for 25 years; there is no marriage equality; and the national human-rights commission lacks enforcement power without a national law.

Documented violence: the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance; activists cite the 2025 killings as an urgent reminder for the stalled bill's passage.

An investigative-journalism investigation (December 2022): transgender women at the capital's main city jail are held by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories with mandatory head-shaving on arrival, informal same-sex “weddings” with male inmates used as a survival and protection strategy against abuse, and safety coming from inmate hierarchies rather than policy.

A regional jail authority, per a local newspaper (March 2023), relocates LGBT detainees in batches to a city jail's annex “to prevent abuse”, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens.
For visitors: no border friction and warm social acceptance, but documented bathroom, fitting-room and resort denials with limited legal recourse, and no partner or marriage-based protections.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via a neighbouring city with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — a 2024 declaration condemned gender-affirming surgery and “gender theory” as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

The custody axis completes the picture: this jurisdiction operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment here serve their time in a neighbouring nation's prisons with costs covered by the authorities here, so there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case in this jurisdiction; any custodial consequence for a visitor would be served in another nation's prison system, outside this record's scope.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Doctrinal and diplomatic context: a 2008 episode saw the national government block a foreign government's first-choice ambassador because he is gay; an educational document (2019) opposes ‘gender theory’ as denying natural difference; a 2023 declaration permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage, with a January 2024 clarification reiterating that blessings never extend to the unions themselves; and the institutional posture against homosexuality drives policy in ways that remain distinct from this tiny nation's own law, which has recorded no modern criminal-law persecution of consensual conduct.

Custody-consequence boundary: a source on crime in this jurisdiction records that the few cells here are used for pre-trial detention only, and that persons sentenced to imprisonment here serve their time in a neighbouring nation's prisons with costs covered by the authorities — so any custodial consequence of an arrest here is routed into a foreign penal system, and no domestic trans-prisoner practice exists to assess.

No resident-facing record exists: no cultural-gender-role, birth-register or resident-discrimination fact is documented for this jurisdiction, and resident jurisdiction itself is essentially absent.

Custody confirms the absence of resident-facing practice: the authorities here operate no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment here serve their time in a neighbouring nation's prisons with costs covered by the authorities, so there is no domestic trans-prisoner placement practice for residents either.

Very small population — the evidence base is thin, and this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty. No source addresses document checks or screening for visitors beyond the recorded absence of border formality, and marriage/partner-travel questions for visitors are undocumented.

Custody axis: no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case exists because the authorities here have no domestic prison system — the sole prison-axis source is a general encyclopedia article on crime in this jurisdiction, used as a last resort because no dedicated custody source exists; how a neighbouring nation's system treats anyone serving a prison sentence there is outside this record's scope.
